metadata.description: Mapping of network attack types to OSI layers and typical security controls that detect/mitigate them. Based on NIST SP 800-61, OWASP, and published attack documentation.

Infiltration.description: Unauthorized access into a system, often through remote login, file transfer, or command injection exploits; adversary establishes presence on target host
Infiltration.osi_explanation: Infiltration occurs at the application level when an attacker exploits business logic or authentication mechanisms; may use transport-layer protocols (SSH, RDP) but the intrusion itself is at Layer 7.
references: NIST SP 800-61 Rev 2 - Computer Security Incident Handling Guide
OWASP Top 10 - Broken Authentication, Injection Flaws

Bot.description: Botnet traffic; infected host is controlled remotely by a command-and-control (C2) server, sending outbound connections to receive malicious commands and perform coordinated attacks
mitigations: DNS sinkholing of known C2 domains
Behavior-based detection of bot communication patterns
Bot.osi_explanation: Bot communication typically occurs over HTTP/HTTPS or custom protocols at Layer 7, but can also use TCP/UDP at Layer 4. Detection focuses on the malicious application-layer behavior and command-control signaling.

Brute Force -Web.description: HTTP-based brute force attack against a web application; attacker repeatedly tries username/password combinations to gain unauthorized access to a web service (e.g., web server login, API endpoint)
mitigations: Account lockout after N failed attempts
Brute Force -Web.osi_explanation: Web brute force is a Layer 7 attack; the attacker sends legitimate-looking HTTP POST requests to a login endpoint with varying credentials. The Transport layer (TCP/HTTP) is used, but the attack occurs at the application logic.
references: OWASP Testing Guide - Brute Force Authentication
NIST SP 800-63B - Authentication and Lifecycle Management

Brute Force -XSS.description: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) brute force or payload testing; attacker sends many HTTP requests with varying XSS payloads to discover reflected or stored XSS vulnerabilities in a web application
Brute Force -XSS.osi_explanation: XSS attacks operate at Layer 7; the attacker crafts HTTP requests containing malicious JavaScript payloads, relying on the web application to render/execute the injected code in victim browsers.

DoS-Hulk.description: HTTP-based Denial of Service using the HULK (HTTP Unbearable Load King) tool; attacker sends many HTTP GET/POST requests with random User-Agent and referrer headers to overwhelm a web server
typical_controls: WAF (Web Application Firewall) with DoS protection
mitigations: CAPTCHA / JavaScript challenge for rapid requests
DDoS mitigation CDN (e.g., Cloudflare, AWS Shield)
DoS-Hulk.osi_explanation: HULK DoS operates at Layer 7 by flooding the web application with HTTP requests that mimic legitimate traffic but overwhelm server resources (CPU, bandwidth, connection limits).
references: NIST SP 800-61 - Denial of Service Attacks

DoS-Slowloris.description: Slowloris DoS attack; attacker opens many HTTP connections to a web server and sends incomplete/slow HTTP requests to keep connections open indefinitely, exhausting server connection limits
mitigations: Configure short timeout for incomplete requests
DoS-Slowloris.osi_explanation: Slowloris is a Layer 7 attack that exploits HTTP protocol semantics (slow transmission) to tie up server resources; the attacker uses legitimate TCP connections but sends data at an intentionally slow rate.
references: NIST SP 800-61 - Denial of Service Attacks

DDoS-LOIC-HTTP.description: Distributed Denial of Service using the LOIC (Low Orbit Ion Cannon) HTTP mode; multiple attacker machines send high-volume HTTP requests to a target web server
mitigations: DDoS mitigation CDN (Akamai, Cloudflare, AWS Shield)
Rate limiting at application & network levels
DDoS-LOIC-HTTP.osi_explanation: LOIC-HTTP DDoS is a Layer 7 attack sending HTTP requests; distributed means traffic comes from many sources, making IP-level blocking ineffective. Detection requires volume analysis and behavioral patterns.

DDoS-HOIC.description: Distributed Denial of Service using HOIC (High Orbit Ion Cannon); similar to LOIC but with improved evasion (random headers, session-based targeting), sending botnet-driven HTTP requests
DDoS-HOIC.osi_explanation: HOIC DDoS operates at Layer 7 with sophisticated session-level obfuscation; each botnet node attempts to mimic legitimate users, requiring behavioral analysis beyond simple rate limiting.

SQL Injection.description: SQL injection attack; attacker sends specially crafted SQL statements in HTTP requests (e.g., form input, URL parameters) to manipulate backend database queries and gain unauthorized data access or modify data
typical_controls: WAF (Web Application Firewall) with SQL injection detection
mitigations: Principle of least privilege (database user permissions)
SQL Injection.osi_explanation: SQL injection is a Layer 7 application-level attack; the malicious payload is embedded in HTTP requests, interpreted by the web application's database driver, and executed on the backend database.
references: OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet

Heartbleed.description: Heartbleed vulnerability exploitation (CVE-2014-0160); attacker sends crafted TLS heartbeat requests to extract unencrypted plaintext from server memory (SSL/TLS keys, passwords, session tokens), bypassing application-level authentication
typical_controls: Firewall blocking TLS heartbeat on specific servers
mitigations: Immediately patch OpenSSL to 1.0.1g or later (or disable TLS heartbeat extension)
Monitor for use of leaked credentials
Enable TLS 1.2+, disable older SSL/TLS versions
Heartbleed.osi_explanation: Heartbleed operates at the TLS/Crypto layer (Transport-Presentation boundary, Layers 4-6) by exploiting a vulnerability in the TLS heartbeat extension; it's not an application-logic attack but a crypto-protocol exploit.

Layer 7 (Application).description: Application logic, web application, database attacks

Firewall-Level.description: Network perimeter controls; packet filtering, stateful inspection, IP reputation
Firewall-Level.effectiveness: Low - most attacks use legitimate protocols (HTTP, HTTPS)

IDS/IPS-Level.description: Intrusion detection/prevention with signature matching, anomaly detection, protocol analysis

WAF-Level.description: Web Application Firewall; HTTP/HTTPS request filtering, payload inspection, rate limiting

EDR-Level.description: Endpoint Detection & Response; malware detection, behavior analysis, process monitoring

SIEM-Level.description: Security Information & Event Management; log aggregation, correlation, anomaly detection
SIEM-Level.effectiveness: Medium-High - depends on log quality and detection rules

notes.generalization: This mapping is based on published attack documentation, NIST guidelines, and CIC-IDS2018 official attack descriptions. It is NOT dataset-specific but represents standard cybersecurity industry knowledge.
notes.dataset_caveat: CIC-IDS2018 may include simplified or synthetic versions of attacks; real-world implementations may show different network signatures.
notes.layer_classification: Some attacks span multiple layers; primary layer is listed as the main locus of the attack logic.
